grammarPoints.title: Advanced passive forms
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use passive infinitives, passive -ing forms, and the 'get' passive to express actions received by the subject in complex sentences.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Beyond the basic passive voice, English uses more advanced passive forms to express actions received by the subject in various contexts. These include passive infinitives and passive -ing forms, which allow for greater flexibility in sentence structure.

*Passive infinitives* (to be + past participle) are often used after certain verbs, adjectives, or nouns, especially when talking about obligations, plans, or expectations. For example, "The work needs *to be completed* soon." *Passive -ing forms* (being + past participle) are typically found after prepositions or verbs that take an -ing form, such as 'avoid', 'imagine', or 'dislike'. For instance, "She dislikes *being interrupted*."

The *'get' passive* (get + past participle) is another common form, especially in informal English. It often implies that something happened unexpectedly, accidentally, or that the subject was actively involved in the outcome, often with a sense of difficulty or consequence. For example, "They *got caught* in the rain." While 'be' passive describes a state or action, 'get' passive often emphasizes the process or the event itself.

examples.text: The new software is *to be installed* by the end of the week.
examples.note: Uses a passive infinitive to express a plan or obligation.

examples.text: He hates *being told* what to do all the time.
examples.note: Uses a passive -ing form after the verb 'hates' to show dislike of receiving an action.

examples.text: My phone *got stolen* while I was at the cafe.
examples.note: Uses the 'get' passive to describe an unexpected, negative event.

examples.text: She hopes *to be chosen* for the team captain position.
examples.note: Uses a passive infinitive to express a future expectation.

examples.text: Don't risk *getting caught* without your passport.
examples.note: Uses the 'get' passive in an -ing form after 'risk' to warn about a potential negative outcome.

examples.text: This order is to be obeyed to the letter.
I object to being treated like that.

commonErrors.wrong: The car needs to repair.
commonErrors.right: The car needs *to be repaired*.
commonErrors.note: Use the passive infinitive 'to be repaired' because the car receives the action.

commonErrors.wrong: She avoids telling what to do.
commonErrors.right: She avoids *being told* what to do.
commonErrors.note: Use the passive -ing form 'being told' because she is the one receiving the instruction.

commonErrors.wrong: They got injure in the accident.
commonErrors.right: They *got injured* in the accident.
commonErrors.note: The 'get' passive requires the past participle form of the verb.

grammarPoints.title: Advanced relative clauses
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use advanced relative clauses like 'whereby', 'in which', 'whose', 'of whom', and 'all of which' to add precise, detailed information to sentences.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Advanced relative clauses allow you to connect ideas more formally and precisely, often providing extra details about a noun. They help to create more sophisticated and concise sentences by combining two related statements into one.

*Whereby* introduces a method or process. *In which* can refer to a place or an abstract context. *Whose* indicates possession for both people and things, while *of whom* is a more formal way to show possession or a relationship, usually with people, especially when referring to a quantity from a group.

Phrases like *all of which*, *some of which*, or *many of whom* are used to refer to a part of a previously mentioned group of people or things. These clauses are typically non-defining, meaning they add extra, non-essential information and are usually separated by commas.

examples.text: The company implemented a new system, whereby employees can access their files remotely.
examples.note: Explains the method or process of the new system.

examples.text: The ancient manuscript, in which rare botanical illustrations were found, is now on display.
examples.note: Refers to the location or context where something was found.

examples.text: Dr. Anya Sharma, whose groundbreaking research was published last month, will give the keynote speech.
examples.note: Shows possession, indicating the research belongs to Dr. Sharma.

examples.text: The board interviewed ten candidates, three of whom were highly qualified for the position.
examples.note: Refers to a specific number from a group of people.

examples.text: She presented several innovative proposals, all of which received positive feedback from the committee.
examples.note: Refers to the entirety of a group of things mentioned previously.

examples.text: The town in which I was born is famous for its old castle.
My eyes are an ocean in which my dreams are reflected.

commonErrors.wrong: The new policy, by which employees can work from home, is popular.
commonErrors.right: The new policy, whereby employees can work from home, is popular.
commonErrors.note: Use 'whereby' to introduce the method or means by which something happens.

commonErrors.wrong: The artist, who's paintings are very abstract, has a new exhibition.
commonErrors.right: The artist, whose paintings are very abstract, has a new exhibition.
commonErrors.note: 'Whose' shows possession; 'who's' is a contraction of 'who is' or 'who has'.

commonErrors.wrong: He has two brothers, both of them live abroad.
commonErrors.right: He has two brothers, both of whom live abroad.
commonErrors.note: Use 'of whom' (for people) or 'of which' (for things) after a quantity to refer back to the noun.

grammarPoints.title: Articles with abstract nouns
grammarPoints.summary: Learn how to use articles (a/an, the) or no article with abstract nouns like 'life' and 'knowledge' depending on whether they are general or specific.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Abstract nouns, such as *life*, *freedom*, or *knowledge*, often do not take an article when we are talking about them in a general sense. For example, we say "Life is short" to refer to life in general, not a specific life.

However, when we refer to a *specific* instance or aspect of an abstract noun, we often use the definite article "the". This is common when the abstract noun is followed by "of" to specify what kind or whose. For instance, "the life of a musician" refers to a particular type of life.

Some abstract nouns, like *knowledge*, can also take an indefinite article "a/an" when referring to a *particular type* or *instance* of that quality or experience. A common example is "a knowledge of something," which means a specific understanding or familiarity with it.

examples.text: Happiness is a state of mind.
examples.note: No article is used because 'happiness' is a general concept.

examples.text: The life of a professional athlete requires immense discipline.
examples.note: 'The' is used to specify a particular kind of life.

examples.text: She has a deep knowledge of classical literature.
examples.note: 'A' is used to refer to a specific instance or amount of knowledge.

examples.text: Freedom is a fundamental human right.
examples.note: No article is used because 'freedom' is a general concept.

examples.text: We need to gain a better understanding of the local culture.
examples.note: 'A' is used for a specific instance of 'understanding'.

examples.text: Life isn't supposed to be fair.
My life is a mess.

commonErrors.wrong: The life is beautiful.
commonErrors.right: Life is beautiful.
commonErrors.note: Do not use 'the' when talking about abstract concepts in general.

commonErrors.wrong: Life of a scientist is often busy.
commonErrors.right: The life of a scientist is often busy.
commonErrors.note: Use 'the' to specify whose life or what kind of life.

commonErrors.wrong: He has good knowledge of ancient history.
commonErrors.right: He has a good knowledge of ancient history.
commonErrors.note: Some abstract nouns take 'a/an' when referring to a specific type or amount of that quality.

grammarPoints.title: As if and as though
grammarPoints.summary: Use 'as if' and 'as though' to make comparisons, describing how something appears or feels, often implying unreality.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use 'as if' and 'as though' to describe how something seems or appears. They are interchangeable and mean the same thing. The clause that follows 'as if' or 'as though' can describe either a *real* situation or an *unreal* (imagined or contrary to fact) situation.

When describing a *real* situation, we use tenses that match the actual time frame. For example, if something seems true now, we use a present tense. If it seemed true in the past, we use a past tense.

When describing an *unreal* situation, we use past tenses to show that the comparison is hypothetical or contrary to fact. For present or future unreality, we use the past simple (often 'were' for all subjects). For past unreality, we use the past perfect. This shift in tense signals that the situation is not real.
patterns: verb + as if/as though + present tense (for real present/future)
verb + as if/as though + past simple (for real past)
verb + as if/as though + past simple (for unreal present/future)
verb + as if/as though + past perfect (for unreal past)

examples.text: It looks as if it's going to rain any minute.
examples.note: Describes a real possibility in the present/future.

examples.text: He acts as though he were the manager, but he's just an intern.
examples.note: Describes an unreal situation in the present; he is not the manager.

examples.text: She spoke as if she had known the secret for years.
examples.note: Describes an unreal situation in the past; she didn't actually know it for years.

examples.text: The old house felt as though it was watching us.
examples.note: Describes a real past feeling, even if the house wasn't literally watching.

examples.text: They celebrated as if they had won the championship, even though they lost.
examples.note: Describes an unreal situation in the past; they did not win.

examples.text: He talks as if he were rich.
She treats me as if I were a baby.

commonErrors.wrong: He talks as if he is a millionaire.
commonErrors.right: He talks as if he were a millionaire.
commonErrors.note: Use 'were' for all subjects when describing an unreal present situation.

commonErrors.wrong: She looked as though she didn't sleep for days.
commonErrors.right: She looked as though she hadn't slept for days.
commonErrors.note: Use the past perfect for an unreal situation in the past.

commonErrors.wrong: They behaved as if they are famous.
commonErrors.right: They behaved as if they were famous.
commonErrors.note: When the main verb is past, the 'as if' clause should also be past, especially for unreality.

grammarPoints.title: Collective nouns and agreement
grammarPoints.summary: Learn how collective nouns like 'team' and phrases like 'a number of' and 'the majority' determine singular or plural verb agreement.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Collective nouns refer to a group of people or things as a single unit (e.g., *team*, *family*, *government*). In American English, these nouns usually take a *singular* verb when the group acts as one entity. However, if the members of the group are acting individually, a *plural* verb can be used, though this is less common in American English than British English.

The phrase "*a number of*" always takes a *plural* verb because it emphasizes the individual items or people within the group. For example, "A number of issues *were* discussed."

"*The majority*" can take either a singular or plural verb. When it refers to the group as a single unit, use a *singular* verb. When it refers to the individual members of the group, especially when followed by "of + plural noun," use a *plural* verb. For instance, "The majority *is* against the proposal" (as a unit) versus "The majority of employees *are* happy with the new policy" (individuals).
patterns: A number of + plural noun + plural verb
The majority of + plural noun + plural verb

examples.text: The committee *meets* every Tuesday to review applications.
examples.note: The committee acts as a single unit, so a singular verb is used.

examples.text: The audience *were* all standing and cheering for the band.
examples.note: The audience members are acting individually, so a plural verb is used.

examples.text: A number of new restaurants *have* opened downtown recently.
examples.note: The phrase 'a number of' always takes a plural verb.

examples.text: The majority *is* expected to vote in favor of the new policy.
examples.note: Here, 'the majority' refers to the group as a single entity, taking a singular verb.

examples.text: The majority of students *prefer* online classes this semester.
examples.note: When 'the majority' is followed by 'of + plural noun', it usually takes a plural verb.

examples.text: The majority of them are decent people.
A number of students are absent today.

commonErrors.wrong: A number of people is waiting outside.
commonErrors.right: A number of people *are* waiting outside.
commonErrors.note: 'A number of' always requires a plural verb.

commonErrors.wrong: The team are celebrating its victory.
commonErrors.right: The team *is* celebrating *its* victory.
commonErrors.note: If the team acts as a unit, use a singular verb and pronoun.

commonErrors.wrong: The majority of the citizens believes in the plan.
commonErrors.right: The majority of the citizens *believe* in the plan.
commonErrors.note: When 'the majority of' refers to individuals, use a plural verb.

grammarPoints.title: Complex prepositions
grammarPoints.summary: Master complex prepositions like 'with regard to', 'on account of', and 'in the light of' to express relationships between ideas formally.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Complex prepositions are groups of words that function like a single preposition. They often add a more formal or specific nuance than simpler prepositions. This lesson focuses on three common ones: 'with regard to', 'on account of', and 'in the light of'.

*With regard to* means 'concerning' or 'about'. It introduces the topic being discussed. For example, "With regard to your application, we will contact you soon." It's a formal way to specify what you are referring to.

*On account of* means 'because of' or 'due to'. It explains the reason or cause for something. For instance, "The meeting was postponed on account of the unexpected power outage." It's often used to give a formal reason for an event or situation.

*In the light of* means 'considering new information' or 'taking into account'. It suggests that a decision or understanding has changed or been influenced by recent developments. For example, "In the light of new evidence, the investigation was reopened." This phrase implies a re-evaluation based on fresh facts.

examples.text: With regard to the new policy, employees will receive an email next week.
examples.note: Introduces the topic of the new policy.

examples.text: The concert was canceled on account of the severe weather warning.
examples.note: Explains the reason for the cancellation.

examples.text: In the light of recent market trends, we need to adjust our strategy.
examples.note: Indicates that market trends are influencing the strategy adjustment.

examples.text: I have a question with regard to the project timeline.
examples.note: Specifies what the question is about.

examples.text: She was unable to attend the conference on account of a scheduling conflict.
examples.note: Provides the reason for her absence.

examples.text: What do you have to say with regard to this problem?
We called off the game on account of rain.

commonErrors.wrong: With regards to your inquiry, we have no further information.
commonErrors.right: With regard to your inquiry, we have no further information.
commonErrors.note: The correct form is 'with regard to', not 'with regards to'.

commonErrors.wrong: The event was delayed on account for technical issues.
commonErrors.right: The event was delayed on account of technical issues.
commonErrors.note: The correct preposition is 'of', not 'for', in 'on account of'.

commonErrors.wrong: In the light for the new data, our hypothesis was confirmed.
commonErrors.right: In the light of the new data, our hypothesis was confirmed.
commonErrors.note: The correct preposition is 'of', not 'for', in 'in the light of'.

grammarPoints.title: Concession
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to express concession or contrast using advanced linking words like 'much as', 'albeit', 'even though', and 'however much' to connect ideas.
grammarPoints.explanation:
When you want to show that one idea contrasts with another, especially when the contrast is surprising, you can use words of concession. These words help you acknowledge a fact or situation while still presenting a different, often unexpected, outcome or perspective.

*Even though* is a strong way to introduce a surprising contrast. It's similar to 'although' but carries more emphasis. *Much as* is used to acknowledge a fact or feeling before presenting a contrasting idea, often with verbs of liking, disliking, or other emotions. It means 'although' or 'even if it is true that'.

*Albeit* is a more formal word, meaning 'although it is/was'. It's typically followed by a single word, an adjective, an adverb, or a short phrase, rather than a full clause. It adds a qualification or a slight correction to the preceding statement. *However much* emphasizes the degree or extent of something, showing that despite a large amount or effort, a particular result still occurs or doesn't occur.

examples.text: Even though it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.
examples.note: Shows a surprising contrast: rain usually stops walks, but we went anyway.

examples.text: Much as I appreciate your help, I need to finish this task myself.
examples.note: Acknowledges appreciation before stating a contrasting need.

examples.text: The project was a success, albeit a small one.
examples.note: Qualifies the success, indicating it was not a huge success.

examples.text: However much effort he put in, he couldn't solve the puzzle.
examples.note: Emphasizes the great amount of effort, yet the puzzle remained unsolved.

examples.text: She continued her research, albeit slowly, due to lack of funding.
examples.note: Adds a qualification (slowly) to how the research continued.

examples.text: I think that Tom wants to do that, even though he says he doesn't.
Tom went to work today even though he wasn't feeling well.

commonErrors.wrong: Albeit he was tired, he kept working.
commonErrors.right: Even though he was tired, he kept working.
commonErrors.note: Albeit is usually followed by a phrase, not a full clause.

commonErrors.wrong: However he much studied, he still found the exam difficult.
commonErrors.right: However much he studied, he still found the exam difficult.
commonErrors.note: However much should be followed directly by the noun or verb it modifies.

commonErrors.wrong: Much as I like coffee, but I prefer tea in the evenings.
commonErrors.right: Much as I like coffee, I prefer tea in the evenings.
commonErrors.note: Do not use 'but' after 'much as' as it already implies contrast.

grammarPoints.title: Discourse markers
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use discourse markers like 'admittedly', 'by contrast', 'as a result', and 'that said' to link ideas and show relationships between sentences.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Discourse markers are words or phrases that help connect ideas and show the relationship between different parts of a text or conversation. They guide the reader or listener through your thoughts.

*Admittedly* is used to concede a point, meaning you accept something is true, often before introducing a contrasting idea. It shows you acknowledge a potential counter-argument.

*By contrast* highlights a significant difference or opposition between two things or ideas. It's stronger than simply saying "however" and emphasizes the distinction.

*As a result* indicates a consequence or outcome. It shows that one event or situation directly caused another.

*That said* is used to introduce a statement that qualifies or contrasts with something you've just said, even if you've just conceded a point. It's similar to "nevertheless" or "however" but often follows an acknowledgment.

examples.text: Admittedly, the initial plan was ambitious, but we managed to adapt.
examples.note: Concedes a point before a contrasting idea.

examples.text: The northern region is very dry. By contrast, the south receives heavy rainfall.
examples.note: Highlights a strong difference.

examples.text: The train was delayed for hours. As a result, we missed our connecting flight.
examples.note: Shows a direct consequence.

examples.text: The new policy is unpopular with some staff. That said, it's necessary for long-term growth.
examples.note: Acknowledges a point, then introduces a contrasting qualification.

examples.text: She's a talented artist. Admittedly, her early work was a bit rough, but she's improved immensely.
examples.note: Concedes a minor flaw.

examples.text: That said, some sentences should be revised.
As a result, the company is expanding its business.

commonErrors.wrong: The weather was bad. By contrast, we stayed home.
commonErrors.right: The weather was bad. As a result, we stayed home.
commonErrors.note: "By contrast" shows opposition, not a consequence.

commonErrors.wrong: Admittedly, it's a good idea, but I don't agree.
commonErrors.right: Admittedly, it's a good idea. That said, I don't agree.
commonErrors.note: "That said" is better for introducing a contrasting opinion after a concession.

commonErrors.wrong: The cost was high, as a result the quality was excellent.
commonErrors.right: The cost was high. That said, the quality was excellent.
commonErrors.note: "As a result" implies cause, not a contrasting observation.

grammarPoints.title: Distancing
grammarPoints.summary: Use distancing structures like 'is believed to' or 'is reported to' to present information as an opinion, rumor, or unconfirmed fact, often in formal contexts.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Distancing structures allow you to report information without fully endorsing its truth. They are commonly used in news reports, academic writing, or when discussing general opinions or rumors. This helps to maintain a neutral tone or to indicate that the information comes from another source.

These structures typically use a passive verb (like 'is believed', 'is reported', 'is said', 'is thought', 'is known', 'is expected') followed by a *to-infinitive* clause. The choice of infinitive depends on the timing of the reported action or state relative to the reporting verb.

For actions or states happening at the same time as the reporting verb, or generally true, we use *to be* or the *base form* of the verb. For actions or states that happened before the reporting verb, we use the *perfect infinitive* (*to have + past participle*). If the past action was ongoing, we use *to have been + verb-ing*.
patterns: Subject + is/are + believed/said/reported + to be + noun/adjective
Subject + is/are + believed/said/reported + to + verb (base form)
Subject + is/are + believed/said/reported + to have + past participle
Subject + is/are + believed/said/reported + to have been + verb-ing

examples.text: The new bridge is expected to be completed by next year.
examples.note: Reports a future event using 'to be' for a state.

examples.text: The ancient artifact is believed to have been discovered in a hidden cave.
examples.note: Reports a past action using the perfect infinitive 'to have been discovered'.

examples.text: She is reported to be living in Paris now.
examples.note: Reports a current ongoing action using 'to be living'.

examples.text: The company's profits are said to have increased significantly last quarter.
examples.note: Reports a past action using the perfect infinitive 'to have increased'.

examples.text: He is thought to be a brilliant scientist.
examples.note: Reports a current state or general truth using 'to be'.

examples.text: Arabic is said to be very hard to learn.
In the past the world was thought to be a disk.

commonErrors.wrong: The problem is believed solving soon.
commonErrors.right: The problem is believed to be solved soon.
commonErrors.note: Use 'to be' + past participle for passive infinitive, or 'to solve' for active.

commonErrors.wrong: They are reported have left the country.
commonErrors.right: They are reported to have left the country.
commonErrors.note: Always include 'to' before the infinitive.

commonErrors.wrong: The building is thought to be built in the 18th century.
commonErrors.right: The building is thought to have been built in the 18th century.
commonErrors.note: Use the perfect infinitive 'to have been' for actions completed in the past.

grammarPoints.title: Ellipsis and substitution
grammarPoints.summary: Use ellipsis and substitution with words like 'so', 'not', 'do so', and 'one' to avoid repetition and make sentences more concise.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Ellipsis and substitution are powerful tools for making your English more natural and concise. They help you avoid repeating words or phrases that are already clear from the context. This makes your communication more efficient and fluent.

*Ellipsis* means simply leaving words out. For example, instead of saying "Are you going to the meeting? Yes, I am going to the meeting," you can say "Are you going to the meeting? Yes, I am." The listener understands "going to the meeting" is implied.

*Substitution* involves replacing a longer phrase with a shorter word or expression. Common substitutes include 'so' (to replace a positive statement), 'not' (for a negative statement), 'do so' (to replace a verb phrase), and 'one' or 'ones' (to replace a noun or noun phrase). Mastering these techniques will significantly improve your C1 fluency.
patterns: verb + so (e.g., think so, hope so)
verb + not (e.g., hope not, think not)
do so / did so / done so

examples.text: Will you be at the conference? I expect so.
examples.note: Using 'so' to replace "I will be at the conference."

examples.text: Did you finish the report? No, I haven't yet.
examples.note: Ellipsis: "finished the report" is understood.

examples.text: He asked me to review the proposal, and I did so immediately.
examples.note: Using 'did so' to replace "reviewed the proposal."

examples.text: I need a new laptop. This old one is too slow.
examples.note: Using 'one' to replace "laptop."

examples.text: Is it going to rain? I hope not.
examples.note: Using 'not' to replace "it is going to rain."

commonErrors.wrong: Do you think it will rain? I think yes.
commonErrors.right: Do you think it will rain? I think so.
commonErrors.note: Use 'so' to substitute for a positive clause after verbs like 'think', 'hope', 'believe'.

commonErrors.wrong: She wanted me to help, but I couldn't help.
commonErrors.right: She wanted me to help, but I couldn't.
commonErrors.note: Omit the repeated verb when the meaning is clear.

commonErrors.wrong: I prefer the blue shirt, not the red shirt.
commonErrors.right: I prefer the blue shirt, not the red one.
commonErrors.note: Use 'one' to substitute for a singular countable noun.

grammarPoints.title: Fronting
grammarPoints.summary: Fronting moves words or phrases to the beginning of a sentence for emphasis or stylistic effect, often creating a more formal or dramatic tone.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Fronting is a stylistic technique where a word or phrase is moved to the beginning of a sentence, away from its usual position. This is done to give it more emphasis, create a sense of drama, or establish a particular tone, often more formal or literary.

One common and effective way to use fronting is with an adjective or adverbial phrase at the start, followed by 'as' or 'though', and then the subject and verb. This structure often expresses a concession or a surprising fact, highlighting the initial adjective or adverb.

For example, instead of saying 'Although it seems strange, the new policy is effective,' you can use fronting: 'Strange as it seems, the new policy is effective.' This emphasizes the 'strangeness' and makes the statement more impactful. It's a sophisticated way to present information.

examples.text: Tired as she was, she continued working on the project late into the night.
examples.note: Emphasizes her tiredness despite her actions.

examples.text: Difficult though the task proved, the team eventually succeeded in solving the complex problem.
examples.note: Highlights the difficulty of the task.

examples.text: Much as I appreciate your offer, I have to decline due to prior commitments.
examples.note: Emphasizes the appreciation before the refusal.

examples.text: Fast as he ran, he couldn't catch the bus that was already pulling away from the stop.
examples.note: Stresses the speed of his running.

examples.text: Strange as it may sound, I actually prefer working on weekends when it's quieter.
examples.note: Draws attention to the unusual nature of the preference.

examples.text: Living as he did in the remote countryside, he seldom came into town.

commonErrors.wrong: Strange it seems, the results are in.
commonErrors.right: Strange as it seems, the results are in.
commonErrors.note: Remember to include 'as' or 'though' after the fronted element.

commonErrors.wrong: Tired as was she, she kept going.
commonErrors.right: Tired as she was, she kept going.
commonErrors.note: Maintain standard subject-verb order after 'as' or 'though'.

commonErrors.wrong: Although tired she was, she kept going.
commonErrors.right: Tired as she was, she kept going.
commonErrors.note: Do not use 'although' in this specific fronted structure.

grammarPoints.title: Future in the past
grammarPoints.summary: Future in the past describes actions or states that were in the future from a past perspective, often indicating plans, predictions, or intentions that may or may not have happened.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use the future in the past to talk about something that was expected, planned, or predicted to happen at a point in the past. It allows us to narrate events from a past viewpoint, maintaining the correct tense sequence.

*Was going to* expresses an intention or plan from the past that either didn't happen or changed. It highlights the original plan. *Would* is often used for predictions, promises, or general future events from a past perspective, similar to how 'will' is used for the present future.

*Was about to* indicates an action that was going to happen very soon in the past. It emphasizes immediacy. *Was to* is more formal and is used for arrangements, obligations, or destiny, often implying a pre-determined event or instruction.
patterns: subject + was/were + going to + base verb
subject + was/were + about to + base verb

examples.text: I was going to visit the museum, but it was closed.
examples.note: Shows an unfulfilled past intention.

examples.text: She promised she would call me later that day.
examples.note: Reports a past promise or prediction.

examples.text: The movie was about to start when we finally found our seats.
examples.note: Indicates an action that was imminent in the past.

examples.text: The new policy was to be implemented by the end of the month.
examples.note: Refers to a formal arrangement or obligation from the past.

examples.text: He knew his life would never be the same after that decision.
examples.note: Expresses a past prediction about the future.

examples.text: I thought Tom would be nervous, but he was very relaxed.
I figured Tom would be here.

commonErrors.wrong: She said she will arrive soon.
commonErrors.right: She said she would arrive soon.
commonErrors.note: Use 'would' to report a future event from a past perspective.

commonErrors.wrong: I would call you, but I forgot.
commonErrors.right: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
commonErrors.note: Use 'was going to' for unfulfilled past intentions.

commonErrors.wrong: The meeting was to started at noon.
commonErrors.right: The meeting was to start at noon.
commonErrors.note: After 'was to', use the base form of the verb.

grammarPoints.title: Hedging
grammarPoints.summary: Use 'seem to', 'tend to', and 'it appears that' to express ideas more cautiously, making your statements less direct and more nuanced.
grammarPoints.explanation:
When you want to make a statement less direct, more polite, or express a degree of uncertainty, you can use hedging language. This is especially useful in academic writing, professional communication, or when you don't have complete certainty about a fact.

*Seem to* is used to express an impression or an observation that might not be a definite fact. It suggests that something appears to be true based on available evidence or a subjective feeling, but you're not stating it as an absolute truth.

*Tend to* describes a general tendency or a common behavior. It indicates that something usually happens or is typically true, but it's not always the case. It softens a generalization, acknowledging exceptions.

*It appears that* introduces a statement that is based on observation, inference, or information, but again, it's not presented as a confirmed fact. It suggests that something is likely true, but leaves room for doubt or further evidence.

examples.text: The new policy *seems to* be causing some confusion among employees.
examples.note: Expresses an impression or observation about the policy's effect.

examples.text: People *tend to* avoid rush hour traffic if they can manage their schedules.
examples.note: Describes a common, but not absolute, behavior.

examples.text: *It appears that* the project will be delayed due to unforeseen technical issues.
examples.note: Introduces an inference or observation cautiously.

examples.text: She *seems to* understand the complex instructions quite well.
examples.note: Gives an impression of her comprehension, not a definite statement.

examples.text: Our team *tends to* perform better when there's a clear deadline.
examples.note: States a general characteristic or behavior of the team.

examples.text: Her health seems to have improved considerably of late.
Tom tends to exaggerate.

commonErrors.wrong: The data is showing that prices increase.
commonErrors.right: The data *seems to show* that prices increase.
commonErrors.note: Use 'seems to' for cautious interpretation of data or observations.

commonErrors.wrong: He is always late for meetings.
commonErrors.right: He *tends to be* late for meetings.
commonErrors.note: Use 'tends to' to soften a generalization about someone's behavior.

commonErrors.wrong: It is that the meeting is canceled.
commonErrors.right: *It appears that* the meeting is canceled.
commonErrors.note: Use the full phrase 'it appears that' to introduce a cautious statement.

grammarPoints.title: Inversion after negative adverbials
grammarPoints.summary: Use inversion after negative adverbials at the beginning of a sentence to add emphasis, often in formal or literary contexts.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Inversion after negative adverbials is a grammatical structure used to create *emphasis* or a more *formal* and *dramatic* style. When a negative adverbial phrase (like "never," "rarely," "not only," "hardly," "under no circumstances") begins a sentence, the subject and auxiliary verb swap positions, similar to how they do in a question.

This structure is not common in everyday spoken English but is frequently found in written language, speeches, and formal declarations. It draws attention to the negative aspect of the statement, making it sound stronger and more impactful.

The inversion always involves an auxiliary verb (do/does/did, have/has/had, be, or a modal verb like can/could, will/would, should/must). If there is no auxiliary verb in the original statement, you must add "do," "does," or "did" before the subject, just like in a question.
patterns: Negative adverbial + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb
Not only + do/does/did + subject + base verb
Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + when/before...
Under no circumstances + modal verb + subject + base verb

examples.text: Never have I seen such a breathtaking sunset.
examples.note: Emphasizes the uniqueness of the experience.

examples.text: Not only did she win the competition, but she also broke a world record.
examples.note: Highlights two impressive achievements.

examples.text: Rarely do we encounter such complex problems in our research.
examples.note: Stresses the infrequency of difficult issues.

examples.text: Hardly had the concert started when the power went out.
examples.note: Shows one event immediately followed by another, with emphasis.

examples.text: Under no circumstances should you open that package.
examples.note: Gives a strong warning or prohibition.

examples.text: Not only were there strong winds yesterday, but also it rained heavily.

commonErrors.wrong: Seldom I travel abroad for work.
commonErrors.right: Seldom do I travel abroad for work.
commonErrors.note: Remember to add an auxiliary verb (do/does/did) if there isn't one.

commonErrors.wrong: Not only she is talented, but she is also very kind.
commonErrors.right: Not only is she talented, but she is also very kind.
commonErrors.note: Invert the auxiliary verb and subject.

commonErrors.wrong: Never I have felt so relieved.
commonErrors.right: Never have I felt so relieved.
commonErrors.note: The auxiliary verb 'have' must come before the subject 'I'.

grammarPoints.title: Conditionals without if
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to form formal or emphatic conditional sentences without 'if' by using inversion with 'had', 'should', and 'were'.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Sometimes, especially in more formal English, we can form conditional sentences without using the word 'if'. We do this by inverting the subject and an auxiliary verb, creating a structure that sounds more formal or emphasizes the condition.

For third conditional sentences, we can invert 'had' and the subject. This structure, like 'Had I known', replaces 'If I had known' and is used to talk about hypothetical situations in the past and their hypothetical results.

For first conditional sentences, we can invert 'should' and the subject. This form, like 'Should you need', replaces 'If you should need' or 'If you need' and is often used for polite requests or to suggest a less likely future condition. It implies that the condition might happen, but it's not certain.

For second conditional sentences, particularly with the fixed phrase 'were it not for', we can invert 'were' and the subject. This phrase means 'if it were not for' or 'but for' and is used to say that one thing is dependent on another, often to express how something prevented a negative outcome.

examples.text: Had I known about the road closure, I would have taken a different route.
examples.note: This is a third conditional without 'if', expressing a past regret.

examples.text: Should you require further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
examples.note: A formal first conditional, offering help for a possible future need.

examples.text: Were it not for the quick response of the firefighters, the entire building would have burned down.
examples.note: A second conditional expressing dependence on a past event for a present/past outcome.

examples.text: Had they invested earlier, their profits would be much higher now.
examples.note: A mixed conditional (third condition, second result) using inversion.

examples.text: Should there be any changes to the schedule, we will notify everyone by email.
examples.note: A formal first conditional, indicating a possible future event and its consequence.

examples.text: Were it not for music, the world would be a dull place.
Had I known the truth, I would have told it to you.

commonErrors.wrong: If I had known, I would have helped.
commonErrors.right: Had I known, I would have helped.
commonErrors.note: To remove 'if', invert 'had' and the subject.

commonErrors.wrong: If you should need anything, call me.
commonErrors.right: Should you need anything, call me.
commonErrors.note: When using 'should' for a conditional without 'if', 'if' is omitted.

commonErrors.wrong: If it were not for her support, I couldn't have finished.
commonErrors.right: Were it not for her support, I couldn't have finished.
commonErrors.note: The phrase 'Were it not for' already includes the conditional meaning.

grammarPoints.title: Needn't have or didn't need to
grammarPoints.summary: Explains how to talk about actions that were performed unnecessarily (needn't have) or not performed because they were unnecessary (didn't need to).
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use *needn't have + past participle* to talk about an action that you performed, but which you later realized was unnecessary. It often implies a sense of regret or wasted effort.

In contrast, we use *didn't need to + base verb* when an action was not necessary. This can mean two things: either you *didn't do* the action because it wasn't necessary, or you *did do* the action, but it turned out to be unnecessary.

When both 'needn't have' and 'didn't need to' describe an unnecessary action that *did* happen, 'needn't have' often emphasizes the regret or the fact that the effort was wasted. 'Didn't need to' can be more neutral, simply stating the fact that the action wasn't required, regardless of whether it was performed or not.
patterns: Subject + didn't need to + base verb

examples.text: You needn't have bought me a gift; your presence is enough!
examples.note: The gift was bought (action happened), but it was unnecessary.

examples.text: I didn't need to bring my laptop to the meeting, so I left it at home.
examples.note: Bringing the laptop was unnecessary, so the action didn't happen.

examples.text: They needn't have waited for me; I told them I'd be late.
examples.note: They waited (action happened), but it was unnecessary and perhaps a waste of their time.

examples.text: We didn't need to book tickets in advance, but we did anyway to be safe.
examples.note: Booking was unnecessary (action happened), but it's a neutral statement of fact.

examples.text: She didn't need to apologize, as it wasn't her fault.
examples.note: Apologizing was unnecessary, implying she either didn't apologize or did but it wasn't required.

examples.text: I suspect that Tom didn't need to be there.
It turns out that we didn't need to do that anyway.

commonErrors.wrong: I needn't to have gone to the store.
commonErrors.right: I needn't have gone to the store.
commonErrors.note: Use 'needn't have' directly, not 'needn't to have'.

commonErrors.wrong: He didn't need have finished the report.
commonErrors.right: He didn't need to finish the report.
commonErrors.note: Use 'didn't need to + base verb' for actions that were unnecessary.

commonErrors.wrong: We needn't have gone, so we stayed home.
commonErrors.right: We didn't need to go, so we stayed home.
commonErrors.note: 'Needn't have' implies the action happened; 'didn't need to' implies it didn't happen here.

grammarPoints.title: Nominalisation
grammarPoints.summary: Nominalisation transforms verbs or adjectives into nouns, making writing more formal, concise, and objective, especially in academic or professional contexts.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Nominalisation is a linguistic process where a verb or an adjective is converted into a noun. This transformation allows you to express an action or a quality as a concept or an entity, often making sentences sound more formal and less personal.

This technique is widely used in academic writing, scientific reports, business documents, and legal texts. It helps to condense information, create a more objective tone, and focus on the action or concept itself rather than the agent performing it.

To nominalise, you often add suffixes like *-tion*, *-ment*, *-al*, *-ence*, or *-ity* to verbs or adjectives (e.g., 'decide' becomes 'decision', 'important' becomes 'importance'). Sometimes, a completely different noun form is used (e.g., 'grow' becomes 'growth').
patterns: Verb phrase -> Noun phrase (e.g., 'when we investigate' -> 'our investigation of')
Adjective phrase -> Noun phrase (e.g., 'it is important' -> 'the importance of')

examples.text: The committee *discussed* the proposal for hours.
examples.note: Original sentence using a verb.

examples.text: The committee held a *discussion* of the proposal for hours.
examples.note: Nominalised: 'discussed' becomes 'discussion', making the sentence more formal.

examples.text: It is *important* to consider all perspectives.
examples.note: Original sentence using an adjective.

examples.text: The *importance* of considering all perspectives cannot be overstated.
examples.note: Nominalised: 'important' becomes 'importance', shifting focus to the concept.

examples.text: We *analyzed* the data thoroughly before drawing conclusions.
examples.note: Nominalised: 'analyzed' becomes 'analysis', creating a more concise and objective statement.

examples.text: In making a decision, I rely not on logic but on instinct.
The doctor's careful treatment of the patient brought about her quick recovery.

commonErrors.wrong: We need to *decide* on the next steps quickly.
commonErrors.right: We need to make a *decision* on the next steps quickly.
commonErrors.note: Using a verb where a nominalised form creates a more formal expression.

commonErrors.wrong: The *develop* of new technologies is rapid.
commonErrors.right: The *development* of new technologies is rapid.
commonErrors.note: Using the incorrect noun form for nominalisation.

commonErrors.wrong: The *assess* of the *perform* of the *employ* was difficult.
commonErrors.right: The *assessment* of employee *performance* was difficult.
commonErrors.note: Incorrectly nominalising multiple words or using the wrong noun form.

grammarPoints.title: Perfect participle clauses
grammarPoints.summary: Perfect participle clauses describe an action that was completed before another action, making sentences more concise and formal.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Perfect participle clauses allow you to combine two sentences or clauses when one action is completed *before* another. They make your writing more concise and are often used in formal contexts. The subject of the participle clause is usually the same as the subject of the main clause.

There are two main forms: active and passive. The active form, *having + past participle*, shows that the subject performed the completed action. For example, "Having finished her work, she went home." This means she finished her work, and *then* she went home.

The passive form, *having been + past participle*, shows that the subject received the action. For instance, "Having been informed of the delay, passengers waited patiently." This means passengers were informed, and *then* they waited. These clauses can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence.

examples.text: Having prepared all the ingredients, she started cooking dinner.
examples.note: Active form: The subject 'she' completed the preparation before starting to cook.

examples.text: Having been praised for his presentation, Mark felt confident.
examples.note: Passive form: Mark received the praise before feeling confident.

examples.text: The team celebrated, having successfully launched the new product.
examples.note: Active form at the end of the sentence, showing the completed action led to the celebration.

examples.text: Having lived in several countries, she had a broad perspective.
examples.note: Active form describing a completed state or experience that influences the present.

examples.text: He apologized for his mistake, having realized the impact of his words.
examples.note: Active form showing the realization happened before the apology.

examples.text: Having uttered these words, he turned on his heel and left the apartment.

commonErrors.wrong: Finishing the report, he submitted it.
commonErrors.right: Having finished the report, he submitted it.
commonErrors.note: Use the perfect participle to clearly show one action was completed before another.

commonErrors.wrong: Having told the news, she burst into tears.
commonErrors.right: Having been told the news, she burst into tears.
commonErrors.note: Use the passive form 'having been told' when the subject receives the action.

commonErrors.wrong: Having worked all day, the bed felt wonderful.
commonErrors.right: Having worked all day, I found the bed felt wonderful.
commonErrors.note: Ensure the subject of the participle clause is the same as the main clause's subject.

grammarPoints.title: The subjunctive
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use the subjunctive mood after certain verbs and impersonal expressions to convey demands, suggestions, or importance, using the base form of the verb.
grammarPoints.explanation:
The subjunctive mood is used in English to express wishes, demands, suggestions, or statements of importance. It often appears in a 'that'-clause following specific verbs or impersonal expressions.

The key characteristic of the subjunctive is that the verb in the 'that'-clause always takes its *base form*, regardless of the subject. This means there is no '-s' for third person singular subjects (he, she, it), and the verb 'to be' becomes 'be' for all subjects.

Common verbs that trigger the subjunctive include *suggest, insist, recommend, demand, propose, request*, and *advise*. Impersonal expressions like *It is important that, It is essential that, It is vital that*, or *It is crucial that* also use the subjunctive. This structure is generally more formal.
patterns: verb (suggest, insist, recommend) + that + subject + base form of verb
It is + adjective (important, essential, vital) + that + subject + base form of verb

examples.text: The committee insisted that he *submit* his report by Friday.
examples.note: Expresses a demand; 'submit' is the base form, not 'submits'.

examples.text: I suggest that she *reconsider* her travel plans.
examples.note: Expresses a suggestion; 'reconsider' is the base form, not 'reconsiders'.

examples.text: It is essential that everyone *be* present for the training session.
examples.note: Expresses importance; 'be' is used for all subjects, not 'is' or 'are'.

examples.text: They demanded that the new policy *be* implemented immediately.
examples.note: Expresses a demand in the passive voice; 'be' is the base form.

examples.text: My doctor advised that I *take* a break from work.
examples.note: Expresses advice; 'take' is the base form, not 'takes'.

examples.text: What would you recommend that I do?
I recommend that you go by bus.

commonErrors.wrong: The manager requested that he *finishes* the task.
commonErrors.right: The manager requested that he *finish* the task.
commonErrors.note: Use the base form 'finish', not 'finishes', for the subjunctive.

commonErrors.wrong: It's crucial that she *is* aware of the risks.
commonErrors.right: It's crucial that she *be* aware of the risks.
commonErrors.note: Use the base form 'be', not 'is', for the verb 'to be' in the subjunctive.

commonErrors.wrong: They proposed *him to join* the team.
commonErrors.right: They proposed *that he join* the team.
commonErrors.note: The subjunctive uses 'that + subject + base form', not an infinitive.

grammarPoints.title: The reason why, the way that
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use "the reason why" and "the way that" to emphasize causes and methods, adding clarity and a more formal tone.
grammarPoints.explanation:
When you want to highlight *why* something happened or *how* it was done, you can use the phrases "the reason why" and "the way that." These structures bring attention to the cause or manner, making your statement more precise and often more emphatic.

"The reason why" introduces a clause that explains the cause. While "why" can sometimes be omitted, including it adds a degree of emphasis or formality. Similarly, "the way that" introduces a clause describing the manner or method. "That" can also be omitted, but its inclusion can make the sentence clearer or more deliberate.

These phrases are useful in both spoken and written English, especially when you want to ensure your audience fully understands the specific cause or method you are referring to. They help to structure information clearly and can make your communication more impactful.

examples.text: The reason why the project failed was a lack of funding.
examples.note: Emphasizes the specific cause of the project's failure.

examples.text: I admire the way that she handles difficult conversations.
examples.note: Highlights the particular manner in which she manages discussions.

examples.text: That's the reason I decided to move to a new city.
examples.note: Here, 'why' is omitted, but the meaning of cause is still clear.

examples.text: Could you explain the way the new software operates?
examples.note: The word 'that' is omitted, focusing on the method of operation.

examples.text: The reason why we need more data is to make an informed decision.
examples.note: Clearly states the purpose or justification for needing more data.

examples.text: I envy the way that Tom can talk to girls.
I don't know the reason why he was absent.

commonErrors.wrong: The reason because I was late was traffic.
commonErrors.right: The reason why I was late was traffic.
commonErrors.note: Avoid using 'because' after 'the reason'; use 'why' or omit it.

commonErrors.wrong: I don't like the way how he talks to people.
commonErrors.right: I don't like the way that he talks to people.
commonErrors.note: Use 'that' or omit it after 'the way', not 'how'.

commonErrors.wrong: The reason for his success is hard work.
commonErrors.right: The reason why he succeeded is hard work.
commonErrors.note: To emphasize the action, use 'the reason why' with a clause.

grammarPoints.title: Verb + object + -ing
grammarPoints.summary: Learn how to use specific verbs like 'prevent' and 'object' followed by an object and an -ing form, often with a preposition, to express stopping or disapproving actions.
grammarPoints.explanation:
Some verbs in English require a specific structure when followed by an object and another action. This often involves a preposition before the -ing form of the verb. Two common examples are *prevent* and *object*.

When you want to say that something stops someone from doing an action, you use *prevent* followed by the object (the person or thing being stopped), then the preposition *from*, and finally the -ing form of the verb. For instance, "The bad weather prevented us *from leaving*."

Similarly, when you express disapproval or opposition to someone doing something, you use *object* followed by the preposition *to*, then the object (the person or thing whose action you disapprove of), and finally the -ing form of the verb. For example, "Many residents object *to the city building* a new highway." Note that 'to' here is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

examples.text: The heavy snow prevented the team from traveling to the game.
examples.note: Shows something stopping an action.

examples.text: My parents always objected to me staying out late on school nights.
examples.note: Expresses disapproval of an action.

examples.text: A new security system will prevent unauthorized users from accessing the data.
examples.note: Describes stopping an action in the future.

examples.text: Do you object to us using your meeting room for an hour?
examples.note: Asks if someone disapproves of an action.

examples.text: The loud music prevented me from concentrating on my work.
examples.note: Explains what stopped an action.

examples.text: Let's not let the lack of money prevent us from doing that.
She tried to prevent the rumor from spreading.

commonErrors.wrong: The loud noise prevented us to sleep.
commonErrors.right: The loud noise prevented us from sleeping.
commonErrors.note: Use 'from' after 'prevent' when followed by an -ing form.

commonErrors.wrong: She objects my dog barking.
commonErrors.right: She objects to my dog barking.
commonErrors.note: 'Object' in this structure requires the preposition 'to'.

commonErrors.wrong: They prevented him to enter the building.
commonErrors.right: They prevented him from entering the building.
commonErrors.note: The -ing form is used after 'from' in this construction.

grammarPoints.title: Were to and should in conditionals
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use 'were to' and 'should' in 'if' clauses to discuss unlikely or hypothetical future events, often adding formality or a sense of remote possibility.
grammarPoints.explanation:
When we talk about future events that are unlikely or purely hypothetical, we can use 'were to' or 'should' in the 'if' clause. This makes the condition sound less probable or more formal than a simple present conditional.

Using *'were to'* emphasizes that the event is a remote possibility or a hypothetical scenario. It's often used for situations that are very unlikely to happen. For example, 'If I *were to win* the lottery...' implies it's a dream, not a realistic expectation.

Using *'should'* suggests a slight possibility, or it can be used to give polite instructions or warnings about something that might happen. It's less strong than 'were to' in terms of unlikelihood but still indicates that the event is not expected. For instance, 'If you *should need* assistance...' is a polite way to offer help.

Both forms can be inverted for increased formality, especially in written English. For 'were to', we move 'were' to the beginning of the clause: 'Were I to win...'. For 'should', we move 'should' to the beginning: 'Should you need...'.
patterns: If + subject + were to + base verb, ...

examples.text: If the company were to relocate, many employees would be affected.
examples.note: Shows a hypothetical, unlikely future event with significant consequences.

examples.text: Were I to accept the offer, I would have to move to another city.
examples.note: An inverted, more formal way to express a remote possibility.

examples.text: If you should encounter any technical issues, please contact support.
examples.note: A polite way to refer to a possible, but not expected, future problem.

examples.text: Should the weather worsen, we will cancel the outdoor concert.
examples.note: An inverted, formal way to state a condition for a future action.

examples.text: If the experiment were to fail, we would need to redesign the entire process.
examples.note: Highlights a very unlikely or undesirable hypothetical outcome.

examples.text: Should you change your mind, let me know.

commonErrors.wrong: If he would arrive late, we would start without him.
commonErrors.right: If he were to arrive late, we would start without him.
commonErrors.note: Do not use 'would' in the 'if' clause for unlikely future events.

commonErrors.wrong: Were she to calling, I would tell her the news.
commonErrors.right: Were she to call, I would tell her the news.
commonErrors.note: Use the base form of the verb after 'to' in 'were to'.

commonErrors.wrong: If should you have questions, ask me.
commonErrors.right: Should you have questions, ask me.
commonErrors.note: When inverting 'should', 'if' is omitted.

grammarPoints.title: What-cleft sentences
grammarPoints.summary: Use 'what-cleft' sentences to emphasize a specific piece of information or to explain an event clearly.
grammarPoints.explanation:
What-cleft sentences are a way to bring special attention to a particular part of a sentence. We move the information we want to emphasize to the end of the sentence, starting the sentence with "What...".

The basic structure is "What + subject + verb + is/was + emphasized information." This structure makes the emphasized part stand out, often because it's new or important information.

For example, "What I need is a new laptop" emphasizes "a new laptop." If you say "I need a new laptop," it's a simple statement. But with the cleft sentence, you highlight *what* you need. Similarly, "What happened was the train was delayed" emphasizes the reason for a situation.

These sentences are very common in both speaking and writing when you want to clarify, explain, or add emphasis to a specific detail or event.
patterns: What + subject + verb + is/was + noun/noun phrase.

examples.text: What I really want is a quiet weekend at home.
examples.note: Emphasizes the desired outcome.

examples.text: What happened was the power went out unexpectedly.
examples.note: Explains the cause of an event.

examples.text: What she needs to do is finish her report by Friday.
examples.note: Highlights the necessary action.

examples.text: What surprised everyone was how quickly the project was completed.
examples.note: Emphasizes the surprising fact.

examples.text: What we discussed was the new marketing strategy.
examples.note: Focuses on the topic of discussion.

examples.text: What we want is a chance to earn a decent living.
What I need is a loan.

commonErrors.wrong: What I need a new laptop.
commonErrors.right: What I need is a new laptop.
commonErrors.note: Always include a form of 'be' (is/was) after the 'what' clause.

commonErrors.wrong: What I want is to buying a new car.
commonErrors.right: What I want is to buy a new car.
commonErrors.note: After 'is/was', use a noun phrase, a 'to'-infinitive, or a clause.

commonErrors.wrong: That I want is a coffee.
commonErrors.right: What I want is a coffee.
commonErrors.note: Use 'what' to introduce the cleft sentence, not 'that'.

grammarPoints.title: Whatever, wherever, however
grammarPoints.summary: Learn to use 'whatever,' 'wherever,' and 'however' to mean 'any' or 'no matter which' in various situations.
grammarPoints.explanation:
We use words like *whatever*, *wherever*, and *however* to express a sense of 'any' or 'no matter which.' These words introduce clauses and show that something is true regardless of the specific choice, place, or manner.

*Whatever* means 'anything that' or 'no matter what.' It can refer to objects, ideas, or actions. For example, 'Whatever you decide, I'll support you' means 'No matter what you decide.'

*Wherever* means 'any place that' or 'no matter where.' It refers to locations. For instance, 'You can sit wherever you want' means 'You can sit in any place you want.'

*However* means 'in whatever way' or 'no matter how.' It describes the manner or degree of something. It's important not to confuse this with 'however' used as a conjunction meaning 'but.' For example, 'However busy she is, she always makes time for friends' means 'No matter how busy she is.'

examples.text: Whatever challenges arise, we'll face them together.

lessons.title: Advanced passive forms
lessons.goal: Learn to use passive infinitives, passive -ing forms, and the 'get' passive to express actions received by the subject in complex sentences.

lessons.title: Advanced relative clauses
lessons.goal: Learn to use advanced relative clauses like 'whereby', 'in which', 'whose', 'of whom', and 'all of which' to add precise, detailed information to sentences.

lessons.title: Articles with abstract nouns
lessons.goal: Learn how to use articles (a/an, the) or no article with abstract nouns like 'life' and 'knowledge' depending on whether they are general or specific.

lessons.title: As if and as though
lessons.goal: Use 'as if' and 'as though' to make comparisons, describing how something appears or feels, often implying unreality.

lessons.title: Collective nouns and agreement
lessons.goal: Learn how collective nouns like 'team' and phrases like 'a number of' and 'the majority' determine singular or plural verb agreement.

lessons.title: Complex prepositions
lessons.goal: Master complex prepositions like 'with regard to', 'on account of', and 'in the light of' to express relationships between ideas formally.

lessons.title: Concession
lessons.goal: Learn to express concession or contrast using advanced linking words like 'much as', 'albeit', 'even though', and 'however much' to connect ideas.

lessons.title: Discourse markers
lessons.goal: Learn to use discourse markers like 'admittedly', 'by contrast', 'as a result', and 'that said' to link ideas and show relationships between sentences.

lessons.title: Distancing
lessons.goal: Use distancing structures like 'is believed to' or 'is reported to' to present information as an opinion, rumor, or unconfirmed fact, often in formal contexts.

lessons.title: Ellipsis and substitution
lessons.goal: Use ellipsis and substitution with words like 'so', 'not', 'do so', and 'one' to avoid repetition and make sentences more concise.

lessons.title: Fronting
lessons.goal: Fronting moves words or phrases to the beginning of a sentence for emphasis or stylistic effect, often creating a more formal or dramatic tone.

lessons.title: Future in the past
lessons.goal: Future in the past describes actions or states that were in the future from a past perspective, often indicating plans, predictions, or intentions that may or may not have happened.

lessons.title: Hedging
lessons.goal: Use 'seem to', 'tend to', and 'it appears that' to express ideas more cautiously, making your statements less direct and more nuanced.

lessons.title: Inversion after negative adverbials
lessons.goal: Use inversion after negative adverbials at the beginning of a sentence to add emphasis, often in formal or literary contexts.

lessons.title: Conditionals without if
lessons.goal: Learn to form formal or emphatic conditional sentences without 'if' by using inversion with 'had', 'should', and 'were'.

lessons.title: Needn't have or didn't need to
lessons.goal: Explains how to talk about actions that were performed unnecessarily (needn't have) or not performed because they were unnecessary (didn't need to).

lessons.title: Nominalisation
lessons.goal: Nominalisation transforms verbs or adjectives into nouns, making writing more formal, concise, and objective, especially in academic or professional contexts.

lessons.title: Perfect participle clauses
lessons.goal: Perfect participle clauses describe an action that was completed before another action, making sentences more concise and formal.

lessons.title: The subjunctive
lessons.goal: Learn to use the subjunctive mood after certain verbs and impersonal expressions to convey demands, suggestions, or importance, using the base form of the verb.

lessons.title: The reason why, the way that
lessons.goal: Learn to use "the reason why" and "the way that" to emphasize causes and methods, adding clarity and a more formal tone.

lessons.title: Verb + object + -ing
lessons.goal: Learn how to use specific verbs like 'prevent' and 'object' followed by an object and an -ing form, often with a preposition, to express stopping or disapproving actions.

lessons.title: Were to and should in conditionals
lessons.goal: Learn to use 'were to' and 'should' in 'if' clauses to discuss unlikely or hypothetical future events, often adding formality or a sense of remote possibility.

lessons.title: What-cleft sentences
lessons.goal: Use 'what-cleft' sentences to emphasize a specific piece of information or to explain an event clearly.

lessons.title: Whatever, wherever, however
lessons.goal: Learn to use 'whatever,' 'wherever,' and 'however' to mean 'any' or 'no matter which' in various situations.
